sketches.title: Alibi for a Bad Dog
sketches.premise: Your pet is wanted for one ridiculous crime, and you are its lawyer. Both players give the same pet a one-sentence alibi; the Judge rewards the alibi that stretches furthest while keeping one crucial fact true. Then each player guesses which alibi matches the Host's real evidence.
sketches.criterion: The alibi must keep the named time, place, and crime consistent, without admitting the pet did it.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence defending the pet while preserving the evidence; example: “At 3:10, Biscuit was in the bathtub, so he could not have stolen the roast from the kitchen.”
sketches.first_card: PET: Biscuit the bulldog — CRIME: ate the mayor’s birthday cake — EVIDENCE: a frosting paw print was found on the kitchen door at 3:10.

sketches.title: Wanted Poster Glow-Up
sketches.premise: The Host has made a painfully bland wanted poster for your pet. Both players rewrite its headline and tagline to make the pet sound thrilling, dangerous, or weirdly desirable while keeping the poster’s facts intact. The Judge gives more points to the bigger transformation that still tells the truth; yes, your dog is a criminal, but at least it has branding.
sketches.criterion: The rewrite must preserve the pet’s name, crime, and reward while changing only the tone and appeal.
sketches.move_shape: Write a headline plus one tagline; example: “BISCUIT: THE FROSTING-FINGERED MENACE — Reward offered for the only bulldog bold enough to rob a birthday.”
sketches.first_card: BISCUIT — WANTED FOR: stealing the mayor’s birthday cake — REWARD: $20 — LAST SEEN: by the kitchen door.

sketches.title: Pet Crime-Scene Caption
sketches.premise: A photo from your pet’s wanted poster shows one ordinary object at the scene. Both players caption it as if it proves the pet is a criminal mastermind, using the two dull nouns on the card. The Judge rewards the funniest leap that keeps the object and the pet’s real habit connected; do not just shout “guilty,” you tiny tabloid.
sketches.criterion: The caption must use both given nouns and make the pictured object evidence of the pet’s stated habit.
sketches.move_shape: Write one caption; example: “The sock beside the bowl proves Biscuit was not eating dinner—he was hiding the mayor’s missing cake receipt.”
sketches.first_card: PET HABIT: steals socks — OBJECT: bowl and sock — REAL CLUE: one sock was found inside the food bowl.

sketches.title: The Pet Who Was There
sketches.premise: A witness remembers two ordinary things near a crime, and your pet’s poster claims it was innocent. Both players write one sentence that links the two things into an alibi, accusation, or suspicious explanation. The Judge rewards how far the story travels while keeping the witness’s one fact true; your pet may be innocent, but it is clearly a little bastard.
sketches.criterion: The sentence must keep the witness’s stated relationship between the two objects true.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence connecting both nouns without contradicting the witness; example: “The leash was wet because Biscuit dragged it through the water bowl while fleeing with the stolen cake.”
sketches.first_card: WITNESS FACT: the leash was beside the water bowl — Nouns: leash, bowl — PET: Biscuit — CHARGE: cake theft.

sketches.title: Wanted for Being Too Cute
sketches.premise: Your pet is wanted, but the poster must make the charge sound like an irresistible compliment. Both players turn the same crime and two ordinary nouns into a short poster line that excuses the pet without denying what happened. The Judge rewards the most charming spin that keeps the charge recognizable; the criminal has cheekbones, apparently.
sketches.criterion: The line must acknowledge the real crime and use both nouns while making the pet seem lovable rather than innocent.
sketches.move_shape: Write one poster line; example: “Stole the cake with a bowl on his head, then looked so damn proud that witnesses paid him in treats.”
sketches.first_card: PET: Biscuit — CRIME: stole a cake — Nouns: cake, bowl — POSTER NOTE: witnesses called him ‘impossibly cute.’

sketches.title: The Last-Known Pet
sketches.premise: Your pet vanished after a crime, leaving behind two everyday objects and one checkable clue. Both players write the final line on its wanted poster, explaining what the objects reveal without changing the clue. The Judge rewards the most vivid conclusion that still leaves the clue untouched; if your explanation is stupid but technically works, congratulations, you are this pet’s lawyer.
sketches.criterion: The line must use both objects and preserve the exact clue about where or when the pet was last seen.
sketches.move_shape: Write one closing poster line; example: “The empty bowl and muddy shoe mark Biscuit’s escape route: he left hungry, filthy, and still carrying the cake.”
sketches.first_card: LAST SEEN: by the back door at midnight — OBJECTS: empty bowl and muddy shoe — PET: Biscuit.
